title: Multiplexed rampbook and occupancy capture
content:
Purpose:
This note collects a practical, repeatable procedure for running throughput experiments that intentionally interleave independent traffic shapes (multiplexing) to exercise occupancy, KV/cache behavior, and microburst resilience while preserving reproducibility. It grew out of flaky runs where single-shape ramps hid contention between session types (chat vs. streaming vs. embed).

Scope and constraints:
- Focus: GPU-backed inference serving runtime (v0.8.x through v1.2).
- Workloads: short-chat (avg 40 tokens), long-chat (avg 400 tokens), embedding requests, and small-rerank queries mixed.
- Goal: stable steady-state throughput measurements with clear failure modes and a reproducible warmup/bootstrapping routine.
- Not covered: autoscaler functional tests, network partitioning chaos.

Definitions / vocabulary we use here:
- Multiplexing: simultaneous client flows with independent arrival processes that share the same model endpoints and GPU pool.
- Bootstrapping sequence: the sequence of inputs and timing used to transition a cluster from idle -> warmed -> steady.
- Occupancy footprint: percent of GPU memory and kernel occupancy attributable to in-flight KV caches + batch allocations.
- Epoch: one measured steady window (see capture windows below).

High-level approach:
1) Create a deterministic input bag per traffic class (seeded RNG) that represents token length distribution, temperature variants, and function-calling vs plain text split.
2) Use a client-side multiplexer that can inject flows with independent Poisson/Weibull arrivals and concurrency targets but with a shared RNG seed so runs are repeatable.
3) Implement a 3-stage run: deterministic cold primer -> staged multiplexed ramp -> controlled plateau capture + staggered cooldown.
4) Record both service-level metrics (latency histograms, throughput, error rate) and heavy-weight infra counters (GPU util, GPU memory, nvtx ranges, kernel-level stall metrics).

Detailed run recipe (example):
- Phase A: Cold primer (3 minutes)
  * Purpose: populate ephemeral runtime state (allocators, CUDA context, kernel caches) without filling KV caches with long sequences.
  * Workload: 30s of single short-chat requests at 10 qps, 30s idle, repeat 3x.
  * Expected: kernel JITs compile, CUDA context created, initial allocator latency spikes.

- Phase B: Staged multiplexed ramp (15 minutes)
  * Minute 0-3: ramp short-chat to 60% target concurrency using linear ramping (client shards: 4).
  * Minute 3-6: inject embedding flow (bursty) at 20% of target throughput for 60s windows every 120s.
  * Minute 6-9: introduce long-chat cadence, gradually bringing total token inflight to 85% of desired plateau.
  * Minute 9-12: apply microburst weaving: every 30s, add 2x intensity for 6s on random shard to provoke queueing/backpressure.
  * Minute 12-15: smooth down to final plateau target (see capture rules).
  * Notes: use the same random seed across runs for burst timing and input selection to ensure reproducible contention patterns.

- Phase C: Plateau capture (30 minutes)
  * Purpose: measure stable throughput and tail latencies under multiplexed steady traffic.
  * Windowing: capture 3 non-overlapping epochs of 10 minutes each. Only epochs that maintain <2% instance error increase and <3% drift in throughput vs start of epoch are considered valid.
  * Capture both per-token and per-request latencies, and GPU-level sampling at 5s granularity.

- Phase D: Staggered cooldown (5 minutes)
  * Gradually drop flows (reverse of ramp) to avoid simultaneous cache flushes or long-tail GC events.

Load generator config primitives (recommended fields):
- seed: integer (must be logged).
- shards: int (num parallel client threads/processes).
- arrival_model: poisson | weibull | fixed | periodic-burst.
- sequence_mix: list of classes with weight fractions (short-chat, long-chat, embed, rerank).
- token_dist_file: path to pre-sampled token lengths used for tokenization consistency.
- streaming_ratio: percent requests that expect chunked streaming.
- session_affinity: boolean (true => maintain KV cache affinity across sequences).
- microburst_schedule: seedable descriptor string (e.g. bursts=2x,duration=6s,period=30s).

Why multiplexed ramps catch different bugs:
- KV cache churn: combined short and long sequences expose eviction cascades that single-shape ramps miss.
- Padding-induced occupancy: embedding flows with fixed-length vectors change batch shapes and drift kernel selection.
- Kernel selection hysteresis: cold vs quantized kernels sometimes chosen on ramp shapes; multiplexing provokes jitter between paths.

Instrumentation checklist (must be collected every run):
- Client-side: per-request timestamps (send, server-start, first-token, last-token, recv), RNG seed, shard id.
- Server-side: per-request route/model id, node id, worker id, model version, batch size, memory usage before/after, KV cache hit ratio.
- GPU counters: util %, mem free/used, CUDA malloc failures, SM occupancy sampling, PCIe bandwidth pressure.
- Traces: 1 in N full traces with nvtx ranges (N configurable; recommend N=5000 requests).
- OS-level: cpu steal, context switches, runqueue length, cgroup throttling stats.

Stability and repeatability heuristics:
- RNG hygiene: store and publish the seed and the token_dist_file used for tokenization sampling. If run-to-run variance > 4% throughput or > 8% p99, rerun with identical seed and compare NV counters to isolate platform drift.
- Epoch acceptance: drop first 30s of each epoch as transient. Accept epoch only if per-second throughput variation < 1.5x IQR and error rate stable.
- Thermal/clock control: prefer lab runs with fixed GPU clock (or at least logged clock governors). Nighttime runs have historically produced quieter thermal profiles.

Quick troubleshooting playbook (when runs disagree):
1) Compare NV counters across runs: big differences in memcpy and SM utilization usually point to batch shape differences.
2) Check for kernel fallback noise: kernel-selection logs will show path flips.
3) Correlate client microburst events with queue latencies; if microbursts map to latency spikes, move to smoother ramp or increase concurrency granularity.
4) If embedding flows cause a 10-20% throughput drop, isolate by running same schedule with embeddings removed to validate packing inefficiencies.

Experiment matrix (minimal set to catalog):
- Baseline single-shape plateau (short-chat only).
- Multiplexed plateau with fixed ratio 60/20/20 (short/long/embed).
- Microburst stress (2x bursts every 30s).
- Session-affinity toggle (on/off) to measure KV reuse gains.
- Padding normalization vs no-normalization (compare tokenization strategies).
- Quantized-path probing: run same matrix on FP16 vs INT8 builds.

Success signals / pass criteria for a throughput claim:
- 3 accepted plateau epochs with throughput variance < 2.5% and p99 latency within +/- 10% of the median run.
- No unexplained CUDA OOMs or allocator spikes during plateau.
- Kernel selection stable (no more than 1% of requests hitting a fallback kernel).

Run artifacts to produce and archive per full experiment: 
- client seed and config (JSON), RNG token distribution file, raw per-request CSV, aggregated epoch summaries, per-GPU time series (5s resolution), nvtx trace bundles, and a short run note with anomalies.

Notes and outstanding questions:
- We still need a small canonical set of token_dist_files representing common customer mixes (conversational assistant, summarization, embedding-heavy).
- Consider adding a signed microburst descriptor format so experiments can be replayed deterministically in CI.
- Investigate a lightweight kernel-selection diff tool to summarize path flips between runs.

Practical tips from recent runs:
- Keep shards > 4 for stable ingress distribution; single-shard overload creates false serialization effects.
- For long-chat, we saw a consistent 8% throughput benefit when session_affinity=true because KV reuse avoided repeated KV recomputation across broken requests.
- Use epoch overlap checks to detect drift: if epoch N and N+1 disagree beyond thresholds, assume transient and mark run for manual inspection.

Appendix: example client config (human readable):
seed: 123456789
shards: 8
arrival_model: "poisson"
sequence_mix: short-chat=0.6,long-chat=0.25,embed=0.1,rerank=0.05
token_dist_file: samples/token-dist-conversational-v1.json
streaming_ratio: 12
session_affinity: true
microburst_schedule: "bursts=2x;dur=6s;period=30s;seed=123456789"

If people run this: please attach the full client config and the server nvtx bundles to the linked confluence page and tag with jira SRV-3421.

Author: Maya Chen (eng-serving-runtime) — please ping me on Slack #bench-harness for quick sync or if you want a run template uploaded to the loadbench repo.
